I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Rental Housing Finance Survey (RHFS)
Description: The Rental Housing Finance Survey (RHFS) provides a current and continuous measure of financial, mortgage, and property characteristics of rental housing properties in the United States. The survey focuses on the financing of rental housing properties, with emphasis on new mortgages, refinanced mortgages, or similar devices such as deeds of trust or land contracts, and the characteristics of debt originations. RHFS included single-family residential and multifamily residential properties with at least one housing unit intended for rent.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

60-Day Notice of Proposed Information Collection: 2027 Rental 
Housing Finance Survey

AGENCY: Office of Policy Development and Research, HUD.

ACTION: Notice.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: HUD is seeking approval from the Office of Management and 
Budget (OMB) for the information collection described below. In 
accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act, HUD is requesting comment 
from all interested parties on the proposed collection of information. 
The purpose of this notice is to allow for 60 days of public comment.

DATES: Comments Due Date: November 24, 2026.

ADDRESSES: Interested persons are invited to submit comments regarding 
this proposal. Written comments and recommendations for the proposed 
information collection can be sent within 60 days of publication of 
this notice to www.regulations.gov. Interested persons are also invited 
to submit comments regarding this proposal and comments should refer to 
the proposal by name and/or OMB Control Number and should be sent to: 
Peter Mateyka, Survey Statistician, Department of Housing and Urban 
Development, 451 7th Street SW, Washington, DC 20410. Comments may also 
be submitted via email to [email protected].

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Peter Mateyka, Survey Statistician, 
Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 7th Street SW, 
Washington, DC 20410; email [email protected], telephone (202) 
402-5873. This is not a toll-free number. HUD welcomes and is prepared 
to receive calls from individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, as 
well as individuals with speech or communication disabilities. To learn 
more about how to make an accessible telephone call, please visit 
https://www.fcc.gov/consumers/guides/telecommunications-relay-service-trs. Copies of available supporting documents for the proposed 
collection may be obtained from Mr. Mateyka.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: This notice informs the public that HUD is 
seeking approval from OMB for the information collection described in 
Section A.

A. Overview of Information Collection

    Title of Information Collection: 2027 Rental Housing Finance 
Survey.
    OMB Approval Number: 2528-0276.
    Type of Request: Revision of a currently approved collection.
    Form Number: N/A.
    Description of the need for the information and proposed use: The 
Rental Housing Finance Survey (RHFS) provides a measure of financial, 
mortgage, and property characteristics of rental housing properties in 
the United States. RHFS focuses on mortgage financing of rental housing 
properties, with emphasis on new originations for purchase-money 
mortgages and refinancing, and the characteristics of these new 
originations.
    The RHFS collects data on property values of residential 
structures, characteristics of residential structures, rental status 
and rental value of units within the residential structures, commercial 
use of space within residential structures, property management status, 
ownership status, a detailed assessment of mortgage financing, and 
benefits received from Federal, state, local, and non-governmental 
programs. Many of the questions are the same or similar to those found 
on the 1995 Property Owners and Managers Survey, the rental housing 
portion of the 2001 Residential Finance Survey, and previous 
collections of the Rental Housing Finance Survey. In the 2027 RHFS, HUD 
plans to collect new data on the types of rental properties owned by 
owners who own multiple properties; new categories of maintenance and 
repair costs, including costs associated with natural disasters; new 
categories of capital improvement costs, including improvement and 
replacement costs associated with natural disasters; and data on 
evictions and the eviction process. This survey does not duplicate work 
done in other existent HUD surveys or studies that deal with rental 
units financing.

Congressional staff

branches about the mortgage finance characteristics of the rental

Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) needs the RHFS data 
for the following two reasons:
    1. This is the only source of information on the rental housing

United States to evaluate, monitor, and design HUD programs.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Rental Housing Finance Survey (RHFS)
Description: The Rental Housing Finance Survey (RHFS) provides a current and continuous measure of financial, mortgage, and property characteristics of rental housing properties in the United States. The survey focuses on the financing of rental housing properties, with emphasis on new mortgages, refinanced mortgages, or similar devices such as deeds of trust or land contracts, and the characteristics of debt originations. RHFS included single-family residential and multifamily residential properties with at least one housing unit intended for rent.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research Report: The Rental Housing Finance Survey (RHFS)

## 1. Verification of Your Description

Your description is accurate, with one nuance worth flagging: the text you quoted matches the Census Bureau's official survey description for the 2015-and-later iterations. The survey has included **both single-family and multifamily rental properties since 2015**, but the **first (2012) RHFS covered only multifamily properties**. So the description is correct for the current survey but should not be applied retroactively to the 2012 vintage.

---

## 2. Who Publishes It and Under What Authority

**Sponsoring agency:** U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), specifically its Office of Policy Development and Research (PD&R). HUD funds the survey and hosts copies of the data and analysis tools on HUD User (huduser.gov).

**Collecting/publishing agency:** U.S. Census Bureau, which conducts the survey on HUD's behalf and publishes the official tables, public use microdata files (PUFs), codebooks, methodology documents, an online Table Creator tool, and a Census Data API endpoint.

**Legal authorities:**
- HUD sponsors under **Title 12, U.S.C., §§ 1701z-1, 1701z-2(g), and 1701z-10a** (general research/survey authorities for housing and urban development).
- The Census Bureau conducts the survey under **Title 13, U.S.C., §8** (authority to conduct surveys for other agencies).
- Confidentiality is governed by **Title 13, U.S.C., §9** — responses may be used only to produce statistics and cannot be released in identifiable form. Cybersecurity protections are cited under the **Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015**.

Unlike some surveys, RHFS participation is voluntary (it is not one of the mandatory-response Census surveys), which matters for understanding its response rates (see §7).

---

## 3. History and Provenance

The RHFS is the modern descendant of a very long statistical lineage:

- **1890–1940s:** The Census Bureau collected mortgage and residential finance data in various forms going back to 1890.
- **1950–2001: The Residential Finance Survey (RFS).** Conducted roughly decennially in connection with the Census of Housing (1950, 1960, 1971, 1981, 1991, 2001, plus a limited 1956 interim survey). The RFS covered financing of all nonfarm residential properties — owner-occupied *and* rental. The 2001 RFS, a follow-on to Census 2000, was the last one; its users included HUD, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Congress.
- **2012: First RHFS.** After the RFS was discontinued, HUD created the RHFS to fill the gap on the rental side. The 2012 survey covered **multifamily properties only**, used paper questionnaires, and was an all-personal-visit operation by Census field representatives.
- **2015:** Single-family rentals added; paper questionnaire eliminated in favor of an internet instrument; mail invitation to self-respond, with telephone and field follow-up ("owner-seeker" operations and administrative-record matching to find owners).
- **2018:** Two-phase collection design; first to use a single sampling frame drawn from the **2017 American Housing Survey (AHS)** sample. Because the 2017 AHS rested on the redesigned 2015 AHS sample, **2015-to-2018 comparisons are problematic** — the Census Bureau explicitly cautions about this break in series.
- **2021:** Sample drawn from the 2019 AHS; collected May–November 2021 with a 2020 reference period (capturing pandemic-era conditions). Summary tables released November 2022; PUF released November 2023. Notably, the frame missed rental properties built between late 2018 and 2020 (~670,000 units of new multifamily construction).
- **2024:** Collected June–November 2024 via the Census Respondent Portal plus field follow-up. Summary tables and PUFs were released **February 19, 2026**, with Table Creator updates following in March and September 2026. New content included questions on **short-term (daily/weekly) rental units**.

The survey runs on a roughly **triennial cycle**, with the sample completely reselected each cycle from the most recent AHS (there is no panel component and no sample maintenance between cycles).

---

## 4. Methodology Summary (for data scientists)

- **Unit of analysis:** the *property* (a building or group of buildings/units under common financing/ownership), not the housing unit or the household. Respondents are owners or property managers.
- **Frame:** rental units identified in the AHS sample (rented, vacant-for-rent, rented-not-yet-occupied, etc.). **Public housing units are excluded** (identified via a match to HUD administrative records), as are transient housing types.
- **Sample design:** stratified by building size — 1 unit; 2–4; 5–24; 25–49; 50+ units — with stratified systematic sampling within geographic sorts (region, state, urban/rural, county, ZIP), targeting ~10% CVs on national stratum estimates. Some strata (e.g., 25–49 units in 2021) were certainty strata.
- **Sample sizes:** ~11,500 sampled cases per cycle, yielding roughly 4,400–5,100 completed property interviews (2021: 11,510 sampled / 5,103 completes; 2024: 11,500 sampled / 4,425 completes).
- **Weighting:** successive factors — basic weight (SMPWGT), sampling/property adjustment (PROP_ADJ), nonresponse adjustment (NR_ADJ), and a post-stratification control to total rental units from the concurrent AHS (PS_ADJ). Final weight = PROPWGT etc. Analysts **must use the weights**; unweighted tabulations are meaningless.
- **Geography:** **national-level estimates only.** The PUF carries limited geography (essentially census region/division and urban-rural type indicators); sub-national analysis is not supported — a major limitation.
- **Disclosure avoidance:** Title 13-driven. The PUF is topcoded/bottomcoded (documented in published topcoding guides), cells with fewer than 3 cases are suppressed, and an Internal Use File (IUF) with fuller detail exists inside Census (accessible only through approved restricted-access channels). The 2021 PUF disclosure review approval ID was CBDRB-FY23-104.
- **Known quality issues:**
  - **2021 response-rate restatement:** the initially reported response rate of ~82% was corrected down to **48%**, then revised slightly to **49%**, after internal research found mis-assigned outcome codes. Weights were re-adjusted and tables updated in 2023.
  - **2024 unit response rate: ~41.5%** — a declining trend that is material for any trend analysis.
  - Frame undercoverage of newly built rental stock in each cycle.

---

## 5. Content and Data Products

**Topic coverage** (per the 2024 release): property value, purchase price, year built/acquired; number of buildings and units; recent capital improvements; rental status and monthly rents; commercial space in residential structures; property management and ownership form (individual investor vs. LLC/LP/corporation/trust); benefits from federal, state, local, and nonprofit programs (e.g., Section 8 voucher units, LIHTC); mortgage characteristics — number of mortgages, origination type (purchase vs. refinance), loan amounts, terms, payment frequency; rental income and operating expenses; and (new in 2024) short-term rental units.

**Products and access points:**
- **Public Use Files** for 2012, 2015, 2018, 2021, and 2024, downloadable in **SAS and CSV** from census.gov, each with a **codebook** covering both PUF and IUF variables. The PUF is structured as linked files: a Properties file, an IUFMaster (admin/geography/sampling variables), and a Catvar file of categorical value labels.
- **RHFS Table Creator** — an online tool for building custom tables without microdata.
- **Census Data API** — e.g., `api.census.gov/data/2024/rhfs` (aggregate data).
- **HUD User portal** — HUD's mirror of the data plus analysis tools.
- **Third-party archives** — e.g., Princeton's Data & Statistical Services catalog (2012–2021) and an ICPSR-archived copy (DOI 10.3886/e222161), relevant for preservation redundancy.
- Methodology documents (full and abbreviated PDFs) and topcoding guides for each cycle on the Census www2 file server.

---

## 6. Users, Uses, and Public Benefits

The RHFS is repeatedly described by Census and HUD as **the only source of detailed information on mortgage financing of multifamily rental properties with two or more units**, and the only comprehensive picture of rental-property finance generally. This matters because the owner-occupied mortgage market is well documented through private and administrative sources (HMDA, GSE data, VA, USDA), while **rental housing finance is fragmented and otherwise invisible**.

**Documented user communities:**
- **Federal policymakers:** HUD PD&R uses it to understand loan origination volumes, operating costs/revenues, and program reach; Congressional staff, budget analysts, and program managers use it to evaluate rental housing policy.
- **GSEs and financial regulators:** historically Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (heavy users of the predecessor RFS) for multifamily market analysis.
- **Academic and think-tank research:** examples include Hamilton Project/Brookings analysis of individual-investor ("mom-and-pop") landlords and Section 8 participation; studies of small multifamily (5–49 unit) ownership and unsubsidized affordable housing; and National Academies recommendations citing RHFS as core infrastructure for tracking housing insecurity. RHFS data underpins the now-common finding that ~40% of rental units are owned by individual investors.
- **Industry:** rental housing businesses benchmark project performance against national norms; investors use it to understand ownership and financing structures.
- **Journalists and advocates:** for evidence on landlord structure, rent levels, subsidy coverage, and pandemic-era rental market stress.

**Public benefit:** it is the empirical foundation for policies affecting roughly **19.3 million rental properties containing ~49.5 million rental units** (2021 estimates) — including affordable housing preservation, LIHTC and voucher program design, multifamily credit policy, and eviction/emergency-assistance policy (its 2020 reference-period data captured COVID-era conditions).

---

## 7. Preservation Risk: This Dataset Is Actively Under Threat

This is the most urgent finding for a preservationist or policy activist:

**On September 9, 2025, HUD published a Federal Register Request for Information (90 FR 43436, docket-linked notice "Request for Information on the Uses of Rental Housing Finance Survey Data")** stating that HUD is "evaluating current needs" for RHFS data and explicitly soliciting comment on, among other things:

> "What concerns are there related to **reducing the scope of, or eliminating entirely, the RHFS**?" and "Are there private sector data sources that provide comparable information to the RHFS?"

This is a classic precursor to defunding or terminating a statistical program. Combined with (a) the falling response rate (48% → 41.5%), (b) the 18-month release lag, and (c) its status as a HUD-funded interagency survey rather than a statutorily mandated Census program, the RHFS's continuity beyond 2024 is genuinely uncertain. There is no announced date for a 2027 cycle in the materials reviewed.

**Preservation implications:**
- All five PUF vintages, codebooks, methodology PDFs, topcoding guides, and questionnaire instruments should be mirrored now. Primary URLs live on `census.gov`, `www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/rhfs/`, and `huduser.gov/portal/datasets/rhfs/`; the ICPSR copy provides some redundancy but coverage of all vintages should be verified.
- The **2012 PUF is not cross-sectionally comparable** to 2015+ (multifamily-only, different design), and 2015 vs. 2018+ has a documented series break — archival metadata must capture these caveats to prevent misuse of preserved data.
- The IUF (internal use file) is at risk of being permanently inaccessible if the program ends; it exists only inside Census.
- Commenting opportunities via Federal Register RFIs like the 2025 one are the main formal channel for data librarians and activists to document public value.

---

## 8. Quick-Reference Fact Sheet

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Title | Rental Housing Finance Survey (RHFS) |
| Sponsor / funder | HUD (Office of Policy Development & Research) |
| Collector / publisher | U.S. Census Bureau |
| Legal authority | 12 U.S.C. §§ 1701z-1, 1701z-2(g), 1701z-10a; 13 U.S.C. §8; confidentiality under 13 U.S.C. §9 |
| Frequency | Triennial: 2012, 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024 |
| Predecessor | Residential Finance Survey (decennial, 1950–2001) |
| Unit of analysis | Rental property (owner/manager respondent) |
| Frame | Subset of American Housing Survey sample; public housing excluded |
| Sample | ~11,500 cases; ~4,400–5,100 completes |
| Geography | National only |
| Formats | CSV, SAS, API, online Table Creator; codebooks PDF |
| Cost | Free, public domain (U.S. government work) |
| Universe estimate | ~19.3M rental properties / ~49.5M rental units (2021) |
| Current status | 2024 data released Feb 19, 2026; future uncertain pending HUD's 2025 RFI evaluation |

## Key Sources
- Census Bureau RHFS program pages: census.gov/programs-surveys/rhfs (About, Methodology, PUF, FAQs, Information for Respondents)
- 2021 and 2024 RHFS Methodology PDFs and codebooks (www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/rhfs/)
- Census press releases: Nov. 29, 2022 (2021 tables); Feb. 19, 2026 (2024 tables + PUF)
- HUD User RHFS dataset page and HUD press release PR 22-242
- Federal Register, Sept. 9, 2025: "Request for Information on the Uses of Rental Housing Finance Survey Data"
- Residential Finance Survey history: census.gov/programs-surveys/rfs and the 2001 RFS report (CENSR-27)
- Research examples: Hamilton Project (2020), Terner Center reports, National Academies (2023)

If you'd like, I can next compile a crawl-ready URL manifest of every RHFS file (PUFs, codebooks, methodology, questionnaires, topcoding guides) for archiving purposes.

I'll research the key risk factors: staffing and budget cuts at HUD and Census, the status of the RHFS's OMB information collection clearance, and recent policy developments.# Risk Assessment: Rental Housing Finance Survey (RHFS)

Research conducted through October 2026, covering the Federal Register, HUD congressional budget justifications (FY2026 and FY2027), OMB's RegInfo.gov ICR inventory, GAO workforce reporting, and press coverage of HUD and Census Bureau staffing.

---

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- All five vintages (2012, 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) remain publicly downloadable as PUFs (CSV/SAS) from census.gov, with codebooks, methodology documents, and topcoding guides intact on the www2.census.gov file server.
- The 2024 PUF was *added* on February 19, 2026 — the archive is growing, not shrinking.
- HUD User maintains its own mirror of RHFS data and tools; third-party archives (ICPSR, Princeton DSS) provide additional redundancy.
- No reports of removed files, altered vintages, or disappeared documentation.

**Evidence for higher levels:** None found.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** All historical cycles remain accessible and apparently unaltered. (Preservationists should note that "accessible" ≠ "archived": the files live only on agency servers that are one budget decision away from reorganization, so mirroring remains prudent even absent evidence of removal.)

---

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- OMB Control No. 2528-0276 is **Active**, expiring **January 31, 2027** (RegInfo ICR 202310-2528-004, approved 01/10/2024).
- Critically, on **September 25, 2026, HUD published a 60-day Federal Register notice (91 FR 60978, Docket FR-7103-N-08) initiating clearance for the 2027 RHFS** — signed by PD&R General Deputy Assistant Secretary Todd Richardson. This means the renewal process was started *before* the current ICR expires, and it signals the survey survived the September 2025 RFI that had floated elimination. The notice even describes *expanded* content (natural-disaster repair/capital costs, eviction process data).
- The 2024 cycle was published on time relative to historical norms (tables and PUF released February 2026, ~15 months after collection close — faster than the 2021 cycle's 24-month PUF lag).

**Evidence for Moderate/High Risk:**
- The September 2025 RFI (90 FR 43436) explicitly asked whether the RHFS should be reduced in scope or "eliminated entirely."
- The FY2027 President's Budget requests **$63M for PD&R's Research & Technology account — a 49% cut from the FY2026 enacted $122.5M** — and states that savings will be achieved "primarily by reducing sample sizes" across HUD surveys including RHFS.
- The 2027 collection is contingent on an ICR renewal still pending at OMB and on FY2027 appropriations not yet enacted.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** By the strict letter of the rubric, the survey is on time with an active ICR and a renewal in process. However, the rubric's moderate tier is the right home for a dataset whose continuation through its next cycle has been explicitly questioned by its own funding agency, whose renewal is not yet final, and whose funding line faces a requested ~50% cut. If the ICR clears and FY2027 funds materialize, this could be re-rated to No Known Issue.

---

## Data Quality

**Evidence for High Risk (reductions in granularity, timeliness, frequency):**
- The FY2027 HUD Congressional Justification explicitly plans to cut survey costs "primarily by reducing sample sizes" for AHS and "other surveys" — a stated plan to reduce statistical precision, even if framed as "maintaining data quality."

**Evidence for Moderate Risk (potential/emerging risk):**
- That sample-size reduction is a budget *request*, not yet enacted.
- Unit response rates are already deteriorating on their own: ~48–49% (2021, after a restatement from an initially reported 82%) down to **~41.5% (2024)** — an emerging, self-driven quality risk independent of budgets.
- Documented series breaks (2015 vs. 2018 frame redesign) and 2021 frame undercoverage of new construction already constrain trend use.
- Census Bureau staffing losses (below) threaten the operational capacity behind weighting, disclosure review, and PUF production.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The planned sample reductions are real and announced but not yet enacted, and the response-rate decline is an emerging rather than consummated degradation. If the FY2027 budget passes as requested, this moves to High.

---

## Statutory Context

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- There is **no statute specifically requiring the RHFS**. It rests on HUD's *general* research authorities (12 U.S.C. §§ 1701z-1, 1701z-2(g), 1701z-10a; Title V of the HUD Act of 1970) and Census's general Title 13 §8 survey-for-hire authority — "vague" authorization in the rubric's terms. Nothing would legally compel HUD to continue it.
- Its predecessor (the decennial Residential Finance Survey) was simply allowed to lapse after 2001 with no statutory consequence — precedent that this class of survey can disappear.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- There is **no alternative data collection that substitutes for RHFS** — repeatedly affirmed by Census, HUD, the September 2026 FR notice ("the only source of information on the rental housing finance characteristics of rental properties"), and the National Academies. Private-sector sources cover fragments (e.g., multifamily agency debt) but nothing comprehensive.
- It has documented programmatic use: HUD states it needs RHFS "to evaluate, monitor, and design HUD programs"; it supports GSE multifamily market oversight and federal affordable-housing policy.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The "and/or" structure of the High tier technically implicates the vague authorization, but the High tier's other two prongs (substitutes exist; no programmatic use) clearly do not apply. The dataset is not statutorily required, yet it is genuinely irreplaceable and programmatically used — the definition of Moderate.

---

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **HUD:** ~2,300 employees (of ~10,000; ≈23%) accepted deferred resignation offers in 2025 (Fox News, citing HUD); an additional 442 received RIF notices during the October 2025 shutdown (HousingWire/Bloomberg); congressional letters cite plans for up to 50% cuts, with PD&R among offices reportedly targeted for reductions of up to 84% (AFGE Council 222 letter, Feb 2025). Well above the "1,000 staff lost" and "40%" thresholds.
- **Census Bureau:** ~1,300 employees lost to DRP/early retirement (AP; AFGE Council 241); the American Statistical Association estimates a **15% staffing loss since FY2024**; Director Rob Santos resigned, the agency is led by an acting director, and 18 top leadership positions were vacant — clear "leadership removed/threatened" evidence. Census's FY2026 request also cut periodic-programs staffing by 27%.
- **Funding:** PD&R's R&T account was cut from $139M (FY2025) to $122.5M (FY2026 enacted, −12%, in the Moderate band), and the FY2027 request of $63M is a **−49% cut** — exceeding the 20% High threshold if enacted.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk only:** The FY2027 budget is not yet law; FY2026 enacted cut was 12%; the RHFS was nonetheless fully funded and executed in 2024 and its 2026 release proceeded normally.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Multiple High-tier triggers are already met (≥1,000 staff lost at HUD; ≥20% workforce reduction; leadership turnover at Census), independent of what happens to the FY2027 budget. The survey is an interagency product of *two* agencies that have both lost substantial staff.

---

## Policy

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The **September 9, 2025 Federal Register RFI (90 FR 43436)** is a formal, published statement by the funding agency that it is "evaluating current needs" for the data and soliciting comment on "reducing the scope of, or eliminating entirely, the RHFS" — squarely "proposed or pending changes / statements suggesting a change is being considered."
- The FY2026 and FY2027 budget requests both proposed large PD&R cuts, an administration-priority signal.
- The 2027 cycle's new content (eviction-process questions, natural-disaster costs) is a notable change to what is collected, though it is additive rather than suppressive.

**Evidence against High/Gone:**
- No termination has occurred; the September 2026 60-day notice affirmatively continues and modestly expands the survey.
- No Presidential-Action-driven ICR and no negative policy note on the dataset pages was found.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** An on-the-record proposal to consider elimination, followed a year later by a decision to continue, is the picture of a dataset that survived a policy review rather than one untouched by it. The Moderate tier ("proposed or pending changes") fits precisely.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

- **Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue** — all five vintages (2012–2024) remain fully accessible and unaltered.
- **Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk** — on time with an active ICR and a 2027 cycle formally initiated (91 FR 60978), but renewal is pending, elimination was formally floated in 2025, and the funding line faces a requested 49% cut.
- **Data Quality: Moderate Risk** — announced plans to reduce sample sizes (FY2027 CJ) plus falling response rates (49% → 41.5%); risks are emerging, not yet consummated.
- **Statutory Context: Moderate Risk** — no statutory mandate and only general research authority, but no substitute data source exists and programmatic use is documented.
- **Staffing and Funding: High Risk** — HUD lost ~2,300+ staff (~23%+) with further RIFs; Census lost ~15% of staff and its director; PD&R budget cut 12% (FY2026 enacted) with a 49% cut requested for FY2027.
- **Policy: Moderate Risk** — the agency formally solicited comment on reducing or eliminating the survey (Sept 2025 RFI), then opted to continue it (Sept 2026 notice); changes remain possible.

**Overall:** The RHFS is not in imminent danger of disappearing — the 2027 cycle's clearance process is the strongest single piece of good news — but it is a **non-statutory, sponsor-funded survey sitting inside two agencies undergoing severe workforce reductions, with a funding line targeted for a ~50% cut and a recent formal review of its elimination**. For preservation purposes, this profile warrants active mirroring of all vintages and documentation now, and close monitoring of two near-term decision points: the OMB renewal of ICR 2528-0276 (expires January 31, 2027) and the FY2027 THUD appropriation.

A. Overview of Information Collection

    Title of Information Collection: 2027 Rental Housing Finance 
Survey.
    OMB Approval Number: 2528-0276.
    Type of Request: Revision of a currently approved collection.
    Form Number: N/A.
    Description of the need for the information and proposed use: The 
Rental Housing Finance Survey (RHFS) provides a measure of financial, 
mortgage, and property characteristics of rental housing properties in 
the United States. RHFS focuses on mortgage financing of rental housing 
properties, with emphasis on new originations for purchase-money 
mortgages and refinancing, and the characteristics of these new 
originations.
    The RHFS collects data on property values of residential 
structures, characteristics of residential structures, rental status 
and rental value of units within the residential structures, commercial 
use of space within residential structures, property management status, 
ownership status, a detailed assessment of mortgage financing, and 
benefits received from Federal, state, local, and non-governmental 
programs. Many of the questions are the same or similar to those found 
on the 1995 Property Owners and Managers Survey, the rental housing 
portion of the 2001 Residential Finance Survey, and previous 
collections of the Rental Housing Finance Survey. In the 2027 RHFS, HUD 
plans to collect new data on the types of rental properties owned by 
owners who own multiple properties; new categories of maintenance and 
repair costs, including costs associated with natural disasters; new 
categories of capital improvement costs, including improvement and 
replacement costs associated with natural disasters; and data on 
evictions and the eviction process. This survey does not duplicate work 
done in other existent HUD surveys or studies that deal with rental 
units financing.
    Policy analysts, program managers, budget analysts, and 
Congressional staff

[[Page 60979]]

can use the survey's results to advise executive and legislative 
branches about the mortgage finance characteristics of the rental 
housing stock in the United States and the suitability of public policy 
initiatives. Academic researchers and private organizations will also 
utilize the data to facilitate their research and projects. The 
Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) needs the RHFS data 
for the following two reasons:
    1. This is the only source of information on the rental housing 
finance characteristics of rental properties.
    2. HUD needs this information to gain a better understanding of the 
mortgage finance characteristics of the rental housing stock in the 
United States to evaluate, monitor, and design HUD programs.
    Respondents: Owners and managers of rental properties.
    Estimated Number of Respondents: 10,000.
    Frequency of Response: One time every three years.
    Average Hours per Response: 1.
    Total Estimated Burdens: 10,000 hours.
